steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is spreading rapidly and it is fundamentally changing how we interact with technology. AI systems now have extraordinary capabilities to generate, compose, and respond in a way that may be seen as emulating human behavior. In the healthcare domain in particular, future trends and transformative projections expect a new era of preventive and interactive care, which is driven by advances in large language models (LLMs). Interactive conversational models, commonly called chatbots, have a lot of potential to help individuals, including patients and healthcare providers, with many tasks such as symptom assessment, primary medical and health education, mental health support, lifestyle coaching, appointment scheduling, medication reminders, patient triaging, and allocating health resources.

Because healthcare applications are life-critical, using conversational models requires a unified and comprehensive set of foundation metrics. These metrics should allow a careful evaluation of the models’ performance and capabilities, identify potential errors, and implement effective feedback mechanisms. Such metrics can lead to significant advances in delivering robust, accurate, and reliable healthcare services. However, the existing evaluation metrics that have been introduced and used to assess healthcare chatbots have two significant gaps that need careful attention.

First, many existing generic metrics lack a unified and standard definition, and there is no consensus on whether they are appropriate for evaluating healthcare chatbots. Right now, state-of-the-art conversational models are mostly assessed and compared from language-specific perspectives and by surface-form similarity, using intrinsic metrics such as Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) and Recall-oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROUGE). These metrics are model-based, but they do not understand medical concepts (e.g., symptoms, diagnostic tests, diagnoses, and treatments), how they interplay, and the priority for the well-being of the patient, and all of these are crucial for medical decision-making. Because of this, they do not capture well vital aspects like semantic nuances, contextual relevance, long-range dependencies, changes in critical semantic ordering, and human-centric perspectives, so they are limited in evaluating healthcare chatbots. Also, some extrinsic context-aware evaluation methods have been introduced to include human judgment in chatbot assessment. But these methods have only concentrated on specific aspects, such as robustness of the generated answers within a particular medical domain.

Gap 2: user-centered aspects ignored
- connection, support, emotion; emotional bonds in physician-patient communication
- attentiveness, thoughtfulness, emotional understanding, trust-building, behavioral responsiveness, user comprehension, satisfaction
- ethics: fairness, biases from overfitting
- hallucination: misleading or inaccurate information; safety and currentness paramount
- personalization vs generalization balance; empathetic, supportive responses
- performance aspects ignored: computational efficiency, model size

What this article does
- review state-of-the-art metrics; exhaustive set of user-centered metrics
- problems addressed, existing benchmarks, taxonomy
- language processing, impact on real-world clinical tasks, interactive conversations
- framework: cooperative, end-to-end, standardized evaluation
- challenges: target audience, evaluation methods, prompt techniques

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is spreading rapidly and it is fundamentally changing how we interact with technology. AI systems now have extraordinary capabilities to generate, compose, and respond in a way that may be seen as emulating human behavior. In the healthcare domain in particular, future trends and transformative projections expect a new era of preventive and interactive care, which is driven by advances in large language models (LLMs). Interactive conversational models, commonly called chatbots, have a lot of potential to help individuals, including patients and healthcare providers, with many tasks such as symptom assessment, primary medical and health education, mental health support, lifestyle coaching, appointment scheduling, medication reminders, patient triaging, and allocating health resources.

Because healthcare applications are life-critical, using conversational models requires a unified and comprehensive set of foundation metrics. These metrics should allow a careful evaluation of the models’ performance and capabilities, identify potential errors, and implement effective feedback mechanisms. Such metrics can lead to significant advances in delivering robust, accurate, and reliable healthcare services. However, the existing evaluation metrics that have been introduced and used to assess healthcare chatbots have two significant gaps that need careful attention.

First, many existing generic metrics lack a unified and standard definition, and there is no consensus on whether they are appropriate for evaluating healthcare chatbots. Right now, state-of-the-art conversational models are mostly assessed and compared from language-specific perspectives and by surface-form similarity, using intrinsic metrics such as Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) and Recall-oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROUGE). These metrics are model-based, but they do not understand medical concepts (e.g., symptoms, diagnostic tests, diagnoses, and treatments), how they interplay, and the priority for the well-being of the patient, and all of these are crucial for medical decision-making. Because of this, they do not capture well vital aspects like semantic nuances, contextual relevance, long-range dependencies, changes in critical semantic ordering, and human-centric perspectives, so they are limited in evaluating healthcare chatbots. Also, some extrinsic context-aware evaluation methods have been introduced to include human judgment in chatbot assessment. But these methods have only concentrated on specific aspects, such as robustness of the generated answers within a particular medical domain.

Second, the existing evaluation metrics clearly overlook a wide range of crucial user-centered aspects, which show how much a chatbot connects with the patient and conveys support and emotion to them. Emotional bonds are very important in physician-patient communications, but they are often ignored when chatbots are developed and evaluated. Healthcare chatbot assessment should consider the level of attentiveness, thoughtfulness, emotional understanding, trust-building, behavioral responsiveness, user comprehension, and the level of satisfaction or dissatisfaction experienced. The ethical implications of chatbots also urgently need to be evaluated, including fairness and biases that come from overfitting. Also, the current methods do not address hallucination, where chatbots generate misleading or inaccurate information. Hallucinations are a significant concern especially in the healthcare domain, where safety and currentness of information are paramount. The evaluation of healthcare chatbots should cover not only their ability to give personalized responses to individual users but also their ability to give accurate and reliable information that applies to a broader user base. Getting the balance between personalization and generalization right is crucial for practical and trustworthy healthcare guidance. Metrics are also needed to assess whether the chatbot can deliver empathetic and supportive responses during healthcare interactions, which reflects its capacity to provide compassionate care. And existing evaluations overlook performance aspects of models, such as computational efficiency and model size, which are crucial for practical implementation.

In this article, we start by going into the current state-of-the-art evaluation metrics that can be used to assess healthcare chatbots. Then we introduce an exhaustive collection of user-centered evaluation metrics. We present the problems these metrics address, the existing benchmarks, and their taxonomy, to give a thorough and well-rounded understanding of a healthcare chatbot’s performance across diverse dimensions. The metrics cover the chatbot’s language processing capabilities, its impact on real-world clinical tasks, and its effectiveness in facilitating user interactive conversations. We also present a framework that helps implement a cooperative, end-to-end, and standardized approach for evaluating the metrics. We discuss the challenges of defining and implementing these metrics, emphasizing factors such as the target audience, evaluation methods, and prompt techniques that are integral to this process.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping our interactions with technology. AI systems now have extraordinary capabilities to generate, compose, and respond in a manner that may be perceived as emulating human behavior. Particularly within the healthcare domain, future trends and transformative projections anticipate a new era characterized by preventive and interactive care driven by the advancements of large language models (LLMs). Interactive conversational models, commonly known as chatbots, have considerable potential to assist individuals, including patients and healthcare providers, in a wide array of tasks such as symptom assessment, primary medical and health education, mental health support, lifestyle coaching, appointment scheduling, medication reminders, patient triaging, and allocating health resources.

Due to the life-critical nature of healthcare applications, using conversational models necessitates establishing a unified and comprehensive set of foundation metrics [1] that enable a careful evaluation of the models’ performance, capabilities, identification of potential errors, and implementation of effective feedback mechanisms. These metrics can lead to significant advances in the delivery of robust, accurate, and reliable healthcare services. However, the existing evaluation metrics introduced and employed for assessing healthcare chatbots [2,3,4] have two significant gaps that need careful attention.

Firstly, many existing generic metrics [5,6,7] suffer from a lack of unified and standard definition and consensus regarding their appropriateness for evaluating healthcare chatbots. Currently, state-of-the-art conversational models are mostly assessed and compared based on language-specific perspectives [8] and surface-form similarity [8] using intrinsic metrics such as Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) [9] and Recall-oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROUGE) [5]. Although these metrics are model-based, they lack an understanding of medical concepts (e.g., symptoms, diagnostic tests, diagnoses, and treatments), their interplay, and the priority for the well-being of the patient, all of which are crucial for medical decision-making [10]. For this reason, they do not adequately capture vital aspects like semantic nuances, contextual relevance, long-range dependencies, changes in critical semantic ordering, and human-centric perspectives [11], thereby limiting their effectiveness in evaluating healthcare chatbots. Moreover, specific extrinsic context-aware evaluation methods have been introduced to incorporate human judgment in chatbot assessment [9,12,13,7,14,15,16]. However, these methods have only concentrated on specific aspects, such as robustness of the generated answers within a particular medical domain.

Secondly, it is evident that the existing evaluation metrics overlook a wide range of crucial user-centered aspects that indicates the extent to which a chatbot establishes a connection and conveys support and emotion to the patient. Emotional bonds are very important in physician-patient communications, but they are often ignored during the development and evaluation of chatbots. Healthcare chatbot assessment should consider the level of attentiveness, thoughtfulness, emotional understanding, trust-building, behavioral responsiveness, user comprehension, and the level of satisfaction or dissatisfaction experienced. There is a pressing need to evaluate the ethical implications of chatbots, including factors such as fairness and biases stemming from overfitting [17]. Furthermore, the current methods fail to address the issue of hallucination, wherein chatbots generate misleading or inaccurate information. In particular, in the healthcare domain, where safety and currentness of information are paramount, hallucinations pose a significant concern. The evaluation of healthcare chatbots should encompass not only their ability to provide personalized responses to individual users but also their ability to offer accurate and reliable information that applies to a broader user base. Getting the right balance between personalization and generalization is crucial to ensure practical and trustworthy healthcare guidance. Additionally, metrics are required to assess the chatbot’s ability to deliver empathetic and supportive responses during healthcare interactions, reflecting its capacity to provide compassionate care. Moreover, existing evaluations overlook performance aspects of models, such as computational efficiency and model size, which are crucial for practical implementation.

In this article, we begin by looking into the current state-of-the-art evaluation metrics applicable to assessing healthcare chatbots. Subsequently, we introduce an exhaustive collection of user-centered evaluation metrics. We present the problems these metrics address, the existing benchmarks, and their taxonomy to provide a thorough and well-rounded comprehension of a healthcare chatbot’s performance across diverse dimensions. These metrics cover the chatbot’s language processing capabilities, impact on real-world clinical tasks, and effectiveness in facilitating user interactive conversations. Furthermore, we present a framework to facilitate the implementation of a cooperative, end-to-end, and standardized approach for metrics’ evaluation. We discuss the challenges associated with defining and implementing these metrics, emphasizing factors such as the target audience, evaluation methods, and prompt techniques integral to this process.
